_purpose: ✒️ Executive Enactment Record — the formal actions, curated from primary sources. Wave 1 (Phase 3) seeded five actions; wave 2 added EO 14156 as its own row and backfilled EO 14151's standing history; wave 3 added eleven actions that closed the largest holes in the record — the tariff program, the drug-pricing orders, the two day-one immigration orders, the digital-asset orders and law, the rescissions law and the fentanyl-scheduling law. Waves 4 and 5 closed the remaining stated-position holes and the two fully-held issues. Wave 6 is the first wave whose purpose is BALANCE rather than coverage: it adds documents that push against readings the file could only agree with, and it declines several that would only have agreed harder. Wave 7 is the first wave whose purpose is TERM SCOPE: every action before it was term 47, so the lane's term filter separated nothing, and it adds eight Term 45 documents — three vetoes, four revoked orders and one law. Wave 8 is the recency backfill: eight documents from April to August 2026, added because the newest order on file had stopped four months before the profile was being read. Wave 9 is the first wave whose purpose is neither coverage nor balance nor recency but STANDING — it re-reads the post-action status layer against the courts' current dockets, appends what had gone stale, and adds the one disposition the vocabulary was missing: `overridden`, for a veto Congress passed the measure over. It seeds exactly one action, the FY2021 defense authorization, because exactly one exists. Wave 10 is the first wave whose purpose is TAXONOMY: it does not close a coverage hole, a balance hole, a recency hole or a standing hole, it closes a VOCABULARY hole. Wave 7 reviewed Executive Order 13957 and refused it in writing because db/issue-keys.json had no honest key for civil-service or executive-branch personnel control, and wrote down that the fix was an issue key rather than a mapping. The key civil_service_control now exists and the five formal actions that belong under it are filed: EO 13839 and EO 13957 from term 45, EO 14171, EO 14317 and EO 14410 from term 47. The key is action-only — no stated position on this profile concerns the civil service, so Axis A reads it as coverage — and no stance was invented to change that. This file is the single source of truth for the lane's action data: the seed_exec_actions_wave*.sql migrations write the same rows into the vr_* spine, and exec-action-data.js is generated from this file by scripts/gen-exec-action-data.mjs. scripts/test-exec-seed.mjs asserts they all agree, so the SQL and the client data cannot drift apart.
_readBy: scripts/gen-exec-action-data.mjs (generates exec-action-data.js — regenerate after every edit)
_shape: Exactly the shape actionsFor() / standingOf() in exec-record.js already read: actionClass, documentId, title, actedAt, term, sourceUrl, sourceLabel, issues[{issueKey, direction, isPrimary, weight, plain, rationale}], status[{status, effectiveAt, authority, sourceLabel, sourceUrl, basis, note}]. `plain` and `rationale` are two different jobs on the same mapping and neither substitutes for the other. `rationale` is the CURATION record: it quotes the sections relied on and can run to a paragraph, because its reader is whoever audits the mapping. `plain` is the DISPLAY line: one tight sentence, two at most, in normal English, saying what the instrument did and how that touches THIS issue and no other. Two rules make `plain` different in kind from a shortened rationale. First, it is written from the FIGURE'S ACT, not from the document — for a blocking class the act and the document point opposite ways, so a veto's `plain` describes the veto and matches the direction issueDirection() reports, while `rationale` and `direction` still describe the measure. Second, where the link is secondary or narrow it says so in the sentence rather than borrowing the primary mapping's force. A mapping with no honest `plain` renders with no explanation line at all; the renderer never falls back to printing the rationale in its place. Nothing here is a new vocabulary — every actionClass is a key of db/exec-action-types.json#actionClasses, every direction is a key of #issueDirections, every status is a token of db/exec-summary-keys.json#buckets.actions, and every issueKey is in db/issue-keys.json.

_sourcingRules.sourceOfRecord: Per db/exec-action-types.json: congress.gov for signed legislation, federalregister.gov for orders. whitehouse.gov appears nowhere in this file, not even as a secondary link — every action here had a primary citation available, so no secondary was needed.
_sourcingRules.standingCitation: Every status entry carries its own source_url and source_label, and a `basis` naming what kind of document establishes it. An action with no citable standing gets NO status entry rather than an assumed one; exec-record.js routes it to unstatedStanding and discloses it as 'with no confirmed standing on file'.

basisValues.enacted_law_published: The standing is established by the enrolled text as published by GPO — the law exists and nothing in the file repeals it. Claims enactment and publication; claims nothing about litigation.
basisValues.court_ruling: The standing is established by a ruling this pass read in full from the court's own opinion. The strongest basis, and the only one that can support 'blocked', 'partly blocked' or 'struck down'.
basisValues.register_disposition: The standing is established by the Federal Register document record, whose disposition notes are the authoritative register of revocation and supersession BY LATER PRESIDENTIAL ACTION. Deliberately narrower than court_ruling: it says the order stands as published and unrevoked, and says nothing about any challenge to it. Every entry using this basis states that limit in its note.
basisValues.register_continuation: Wave 2. The standing is established by a Federal Register notice continuing a time-limited authority — specifically a National Emergencies Act declaration, which expires one year after it is declared unless the President continues it (50 U.S.C. 1622(d)). Separated from register_disposition because it answers a different question: not 'has this been revoked' but 'has this lapsed'. It carries the same limit — a continuation is a presidential act and says nothing about any challenge to the order. WAVE 11 EXTENDS IT TO THE MIRROR CASE, which is the same question with the opposite answer: a directive whose operative authority runs to a date fixed in its own published text, where the register carries no continuation and no later instrument extending it. There the basis supports `expired` rather than `in_force`, and it rests on the same two readings — the document's own timetable, plus the absence of any register entry extending it. The alternative was to file such a directive as `in_force` on the strength of an absent revocation, which asserts something the record does not say. It carries the identical limit: it is a statement about the document's own timetable and says nothing about any challenge to it.
basisValues.pending_litigation: Wave 2, and the ONLY basis that may support challenged_unverified. The row is established by a primary court filing showing a live challenge — a complaint or docket document read in this pass — and by the absence of any ruling resolving it in the same docket. It is strictly weaker than court_ruling and can never support blocked, partly blocked or struck down: a complaint is an allegation, and this basis reports that the allegation is on file and unresolved, not that it is correct. Every entry using this basis names the case, the court, and what the docket did and did not contain when it was read.
basisValues.congressional_action_record: Wave 7, and the basis that exists because a veto's standing is a question no other basis answers. The four earlier bases all ask what happened to a document AFTER it took effect — was it revoked, did it lapse, did a court reach it. A veto is the opposite kind of object: the question is whether the measure it blocked ever took effect at all, and the only record that settles that is the chamber's own subsequent action on the same measure under Article I, section 7. The row is established by the legislative action history for that measure as published by Congress, naming the date the veto was received, the chamber that attempted the override and the result of that attempt. It is narrow in exactly the way register_disposition is narrow: it says whether the measure became law and says nothing about any challenge to the veto or to anything the veto preserved. WAVE 9 EXTENDS IT, and it is the only basis that may support `overridden`: where the same records show the measure WAS passed over the objections of the President in both chambers, the same source that establishes a failed override establishes a successful one, and the enrolled text published by GPO carries both reconsideration resolutions and the approval date.

_whyNoScore: There is no score field anywhere in this file and no count that could become one. See exec-record.js's header: the set of orders a president could have signed is unbounded and self-chosen, so any ratio computed over these rows would divide by a number we picked.

Federal Register facts come from the FR API document records (title, signing date, publication date, FR citation, document number, disposition notes). Public Law facts come from GPO's published PLAW packages. Standing facts come from the courts' own opinions and orders, downloaded as PDF and read — the operative disposition, not a summary of it.

wave2.added: EO 14156 (own row, three status rows), EO 14151 (three appended status rows), and the challenged_unverified standing token.
wave2.courtSources: courtlistener.com's HTML site also returns HTTP 403 to this environment and its docket-entries API requires credentials, so dockets were read through the unauthenticated search API (type=r, fielded queries) and every document was then downloaded in full from storage.courtlistener.com and read as text. Wash. docket for EO 14156 was queried for injunction / dismissal / order entries and returned only pro hac vice orders, and the docket is not terminated — hence challenged_unverified rather than a ruling token; (2) the FR disposition record for EO 14156 contains no revocation entry. wave3.added: Eleven actions: EO 14257 (the reciprocal-tariff order), EO 14273 and EO 14297 (drug pricing), EO 14233 and EO 14178 (digital assets), EO 14221 (healthcare price transparency), EO 14165 and EO 14159 (the two day-one immigration orders), Public Law 119-26 (fentanyl scheduling), Public Law 119-27 (payment stablecoins) and Public Law 119-28 (rescissions).
wave3.why: The executive-lane audit found the same shape of failure eleven times over: a stated position with real formal action behind it and nothing on file to test it, so the lane reported 'no action on file yet' about the best-documented parts of this presidency. The tariff program in particular was the single largest hole — five stated positions, one of which names the order by number, and not one document in the record.
wave3.registerFacts: Every executive order below was read from its own Federal Register API document record in this pass: title, signing date, publication date, FR citation, FR document number and disposition notes. The disposition notes were checked individually for each of the eight orders. None of the eight carries a Revokes-of-itself or Superseded-by entry, which is what the register_disposition standings assert and the limit of what they assert. EO 14273 and EO 14297 cross-reference each other; EO 14159 revokes four Biden-era orders; EO 14178 revokes EO 14067; EO 14233 and EO 14165 carry no disposition note at all.
wave3.lawCitations: The three public laws are cited to congress.gov because db/exec-action-types.json#actionClasses.signed_law names congress.gov as the source of record for enacted legislation, and every existing law row in this file follows that rule. congress.gov still returns HTTP 403 to this environment, so — exactly as in wave 1 — the FACTS asserted about each law (its short title, its approval date, its bill vehicle, the section relied on) were verified against GPO's published PLAW package, and each row records which package was read.
wave3.courtSource: The EO 14257 struck_down standing was read from the Supreme Court's own slip opinion in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, No. 24-1287, downloaded from supremecourt.gov and read in full — the syllabus holding and the judgment paragraph of the opinion of the Court, not a summary of either. The prior pass could not read this PDF and the order would otherwise have shipped with no standing at all, which under consistency.js#execRecordsFor holds every one of its mappings back as no_standing: the largest action in the file would have entered as coverage and scored nothing.
wave3.whatWasLeftOut: Two mappings that would have been easy and are not honest. EO 14257 is NOT mapped to cost_living: whether a tariff raises household prices in the aggregate is a contested economic claim, not something the order's text establishes, and the lane only carries what a document says. Public Law 119-28 is NOT mapped to national_debt: a rescission of roughly nine billion dollars in budget authority and a five-trillion-dollar increase in the statutory debt limit are not commensurable, and carrying both on that issue at comparable weights would have read as a balanced record where the record is not balanced. Its cut_spending mapping is the true one and is kept.

wave6.purpose: BALANCE, NOT VOLUME. Waves 3 through 5 densified the record and the density made a defect visible: of the 32 issue keys in the lane, 31 held mappings that all pointed the same way, and 20 of the 21 issues the audit could test read exactly 100. That is not a finding about a presidency, it is a finding about a collection. Every action added or amended here was selected because it can push an issue off a one-direction reading, and several documents that would have been easy to add were left out precisely because they could not.
wave6.added: Four actions and one amendment. EO 14360 (agricultural products taken out of the reciprocal tariff, with refunds); Proclamation 11038 (countervailing-duty collection suspended on Moroccan phosphate fertilizer); Proclamation 11012 (the section 122 import surcharge — same-direction, and see below); Public Law 119-37 (the continuing appropriations Act whose section 120 bars reductions in force and voids those already taken). The amendment adds a tariffs_prices mapping to Proclamation 11010, which wave 5 declined to write.
wave6.whyProclamation11010Changed: Wave 5's refusal was not overridden, its stated condition was met. It declined to map the beef tariff-rate quota to any tariffs_* issue on the ground that 'filing it under a tariff issue would make the trade record read as though it pointed both ways on the strength of one grocery measure.' Wave 6 adds two further barrier-lowering documents, so the direction no longer rests on one measure. Had those two documents not existed, the refusal would have stood.
wave6.whyASameDirectionRowIsHere: Proclamation 11012 advances the tariff issues that were already one-directional, which is exactly what this wave otherwise refuses to do. It is here because omitting it would have made this wave dishonest in the other direction. On February 20, 2026 the Supreme Court held the emergency statute does not authorize tariffs, EO 14389 ended the duties nine orders had imposed under it, and this proclamation imposed a new 10 percent surcharge under section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. A file that recorded the ending and not the replacement would have published a retreat that did not happen. Its weight cost to the balance of the trade cluster is real and was accepted.
wave6.whyEO14389IsStillNotAnAction: Executive Order 14389 was reviewed in full in this pass for exactly this question and is deliberately still carried only as an Axis B standing, on EO 14195's superseded row. It ends the ad valorem duties imposed under the emergency statute by nine orders, and it is the direct consequence of losing Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump the same day. Filing a compelled compliance document as an issue mapping would tell a reader that the President acted against his own stated tariff position, when what happened is that the Court held he lacked the authority and he re-imposed a surcharge under another statute within hours. Axis B is where an outcome imposed on an action belongs; Axis A is for what the figure chose. The two barrier-lowering documents that ARE filed here — EO 14360 and Proclamation 11038 — were chosen because nothing compelled either of them.
wave6.sourcesRead: Federal Register API document records, one document at a time, for title, signing date, publication date, citation, document number and disposition notes: EO 14360 (signed 2025-11-14, published 2025-11-25, 90 FR 54091, doc 2025-21203), Proclamation 11012 (signed 2026-02-20, published 2026-02-25, 91 FR 9339, doc 2026-03824) and Proclamation 11038 (signed 2026-06-29, published 2026-07-02, 91 FR 40855, doc 2026-13588); the full text of all three was read from the register's own raw-text URLs. EO 14360's forward cross-reference to the notice of March 24, 2026 (91 FR 15517) was opened and read: it continues the national emergency declared in EO 14257 and revokes nothing. For the law, GPO's PLAW-119publ37 package was downloaded and read — section 120 and section 106(3) verbatim. GPO's PLAW-119publ98 package was also read in full and then declined, for the reason below. The full listing of all 102 public laws of the 119th Congress was enumerated from GPO bulkdata to choose among the spending vehicles rather than take the first one found. whitehouse.gov appears nowhere in this wave.
wave6.theSharedIssueRowConstraint: A STRUCTURAL LIMIT THIS WAVE RAN INTO AND THE NEXT ONE NEEDS TO KNOW ABOUT. The 🏛️ and ✒️ lanes do not have separate issue tables. vr_measure_issues is keyed on (measure_id, issue_key), and an executive action on a signed law reuses the SAME vr_measures row the roll-call lane created for the bill. So an issue mapping written for the executive lane is also read by the roll-call lane, and lands on every member who voted on that measure. That is fine where the two lanes agree and it is a silent contradiction where they do not. It is why Public Law 119-98 is not in this wave: see below.
wave6.whatWasLeftOut: Seven candidates were reviewed and rejected. (1) EO 14389 — see above; compelled compliance, kept on Axis B. (2) PUBLIC LAW 119-98, THE SECURE AMERICA ACT, and this is the rejection that cost the most. It is the second-largest signed law of the term, it appropriates $69,545,000,000 out of the Treasury with no offset, rescission or revenue provision anywhere in its two titles, and on its face it grows the federal workforce — a real counter-directional fact against cut_spending, drafted and ready to file. It is not filed because S. 2 already exists in vr_measures with four roll calls and hundreds of attributed member votes, and 20260821000000_vr_secure_america_act_rollcalls.sql declined cut_spending and national_debt on that measure deliberately and in writing: 'Scoring the roll on a spending axis without the score would be an inference, and it would read every yea as pro-spending and every nay as fiscally conservative regardless of the reason either was given.' Because the two lanes share vr_measure_issues, writing the executive mapping would have re-scored every one of those members on an axis the roll-call pass refused. The executive-lane case is stronger than the roll-call case — there is one signer, not five hundred voters — but it cannot be filed on a shared row, and inventing a second measure row for the same law to get around it would put a duplicate S. 2 in the spine. Filing this honestly needs a per-lane issue mapping, which is a schema change and not this wave's job. (3) tariffs_authority was left one-directional. Proclamation 11012's move from an open-ended emergency claim to section 122, which caps the rate at 15 percent, caps the term at 150 days and lets only an Act of Congress extend it, is the closest thing to a counter-directional fact available on that issue — and it was rejected because a change of statutory vehicle made on the day the previous authority was struck down, keeping every decision in the President's hands, is not evidence of deference to Congress. That issue is reported as still one-directional rather than balanced by inference. (4) tariffs_china was left one-directional. Neither barrier-lowering document is country-specific and the surcharge is not either; nothing on file cuts the other way on that key. (5) The three fiscal-year appropriations Acts — PL 119-74, PL 119-75 and PL 119-86 — were read and not filed. Their counter-directional content would have to be an aggregate spending level characterized from thousands of pages, and characterizing a total is not the same as quoting a provision; PL 119-37 section 120 does the same work with text that can be quoted. (6) national_debt was left with its single row. An appropriation's deficit effect depends on offsets and outlay timing that are not in any enrolled text read here, and the lane does not carry contested economic inference — the same rule that keeps EO 14257 off cost_living and the Rescissions Act off national_debt. (7) EO 14345, EO 14346, EO 14358 and Proclamation 10999 — the trade-agreement implementation documents — were seen in the register listing and not pursued in this pass. Each lowers rates pursuant to a negotiated arrangement, which is the tariff being used as leverage rather than abandoned, and reading them as retreats would have been the easy wrong answer. They are named here so the next pass knows they were seen and why they were passed over.

wave7.purpose: TERM SCOPE. Every one of the 40 actions this file carried before this wave was signed or issued in 2025 or 2026 and every one was tagged term 47. The lane therefore had a term filter that could not filter anything: all_time and current_term returned the same set, and the profile was placing second-term effort next to first-term results — four of the eleven tracked promises are marked broken, and the evidence behind all four is from the first term, where the file held nothing. This wave puts eight real Term 45 documents on file. It is the first wave in which the term field means something.
wave7.added: Eight actions, all term 45. Three vetoes — H.J. Res. 46 (termination of the border emergency, vetoed March 15, 2019), S.J. Res. 7 (Yemen hostilities war-powers direction, vetoed April 16, 2019) and S.J. Res. 68 (Iran hostilities war-powers direction, vetoed May 6, 2020). Four executive orders that were later revoked and are filed with rescinded standings — EO 13765 (ACA burden minimization), EO 13767 (border wall and immigration enforcement), EO 13783 (energy independence and the Clean Power Plan review) and EO 13950 (race and sex stereotyping in federal training and contracting). One signed law — Public Law 116-136, the CARES Act.
wave7.whyVetoesFirst: The vetoed_law action class has existed in db/exec-action-types.json since the vocabulary was written and no row had ever used it. A veto is the cleanest instrument in the executive vocabulary: one actor, one decision, a dated document and a recorded congressional answer to it. It is also the only class whose Axis B question is not 'what happened to this afterwards' but 'did the thing it blocked ever take effect', which is why this wave had to add a basis value rather than reuse one.
wave7.vetoDirectionConvention: READ THIS BEFORE EDITING ANY VETO ROW. The direction on a veto's issue mapping describes what the VETOED MEASURE would have done to the issue, not what the veto did. This is not a stylistic choice: consistency.js#_EXEC_BLOCKS marks vetoed_law as a blocking class and sets advanceInverted on the item, and stance-helpers.js flips the direction on that flag. The column being mirrored is vr_measure_issues.support_meaning, which describes the measure. Writing 'advances' here to mean 'the veto advanced the issue' would invert every veto in the file. Each veto row below states the inversion in its own rationale so the mistake cannot be made silently from the data alone.
wave7.theInversionBugTheseVetoesExposed: FOUND AND FIXED WHILE SEEDING, and recorded because the next blocking class will hit it again. consistency.js had handled the inversion since the vocabulary was written (_EXEC_BLOCKS -> advanceInverted -> stance-helpers), but exec-record.js#executiveIssue counted the mapping direction raw. For six waves that was harmless: no row used a blocking class, so the document's direction and the act's direction could never disagree. The first three vetoes made them disagree, and the failure was the flattering kind rather than the loud kind — the veto of H.J. Res. 46 was counted as an action AGAINST border_security, sitting next to Executive Order 13767, so an issue with seven documents all pointing one way read 'Acted both ways' off two of them. The fix is a 'blocks: true' flag on the vetoed_law class and one issueDirection() helper that every direction read goes through; the per-issue result now also carries mappedDirection and inverted so a surface can show its work. No formula changed and no percentage moved — exec-record.js has never had a score. The seed test pins both halves: a blocking class must invert, and a non-blocking class must not.
wave7.sourcesRead: For the three vetoes: GPO's BILLSTATUS bulkdata for the 116th Congress (BILLSTATUS-116-hjres and BILLSTATUS-116-sjres), downloaded and parsed in this pass. All eight joint resolutions vetoed in the 116th Congress were enumerated from that data before three were chosen, and the veto date, the override attempt, the chamber and the recorded result were read from the legislative action history of each. congress.gov itself still returns HTTP 403 to this environment; the bill pages are cited as the source of record because db/exec-action-types.json names them as such, and the facts were verified against GPO, which is the same discipline waves 1 and 3 used for public laws. For the four orders: the Federal Register API document record of each, one at a time — EO 13765 (signed 2017-01-20, published 2017-01-24, 82 FR 8351, doc 2017-01799), EO 13767 (signed 2017-01-25, published 2017-01-30, 82 FR 8793, doc 2017-02095), EO 13783 (signed 2017-03-28, published 2017-03-31, 82 FR 16093, doc 2017-06576) and EO 13950 (signed 2020-09-22, published 2020-09-28, 85 FR 60683, doc 2020-21534) — plus the full text of each from the register's own raw-text URLs. Every rescinded standing below quotes the disposition note verbatim. For the law: GPO's PLAW-116publ136 package, downloaded and read; section 5001 and section 4003 were read in full. whitehouse.gov appears nowhere in this wave.
wave7.whyTheseFourOrdersAndNotMore: Two hundred twenty-nine executive orders were signed in the first term. This wave files four. The filter was not importance, it was whether the document's disposition is unambiguous and whether the issue it lands on is already in the lane: each of the four carries a plain 'Revoked by' entry in the register's own disposition record, and each lands on an issue that already holds second-term action. Three of the four sit on issues that read as fully aligned — border_security, end_dei, energy_production and climate_action — and they do not change that alignment. They change the other axis: those issues now hold a document that no longer stands, which is the contrast the term filter exists to show and which no amount of second-term density could produce.
wave7.theOverrideGap: A STRUCTURAL FINDING THIS WAVE COULD NOT FIX, stated the way wave 6 stated the shared-row constraint. Of the eight joint resolutions vetoed in the 116th Congress, seven vetoes were sustained and one was overridden: H.R. 6395, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, vetoed December 23, 2020 and enacted over the veto on January 1, 2021. That is the single most consequential veto of the term and it is not in this file, because Axis B has no token for it. The vocabulary in db/exec-summary-keys.json#buckets.actions offers in_force, partly_blocked, blocked, struck_down, rescinded, challenged_unverified, superseded and expired. Filing an override as blocked or struck_down would name a court as the actor when the actor was Congress. Filing it as superseded would be the worse error, because superseded is marked contested:false — the most contested outcome available to an executive action would be counted as an uncontested one. Filing it as in_force would be false. The honest token is 'overridden', contested:true, and adding it is not a data change: exec-record.js hardcodes the standing order and exec-record-ui.js hardcodes the chip and its CSS, so it is read-path and UI work. Recorded here so the next pass does not rediscover it.
wave7.whatWasLeftOut: Nine candidates were reviewed and rejected. (1) H.R. 6395 — see theOverrideGap; the only overridden veto, and unfileable without a new Axis B token. (2) S.J. Res. 54, the second border-emergency termination of 2019, vetoed October 15 and sustained October 17. It is the same fight as H.J. Res. 46 on the same issue in the same direction; filing both would put two same-direction rows on an issue that already reads fully aligned, which is the volume this pass was told not to add. (3), (4) and (5) S.J. Res. 36, S.J. Res. 37 and S.J. Res. 38 — three arms-sale disapproval resolutions vetoed the same day, July 24, 2019, all sustained July 29. There is no honest axis for them: the issue they turn on is whether Congress controls arms exports, which is checks_balances, and this figure has no stated position on that key. They are also three near-identical documents, and filing three rows for one decision would inflate the count without adding a fact. (6) H.J. Res. 76, the disapproval of the borrower-defense rule, vetoed May 29, 2020 and sustained June 26. Its only honest issue is edu_college_cost, which carries no stated position, so the row would test nothing. (7) EO 13957, Creating Schedule F in the Excepted Service, and this is the rejection that cost the most in this wave. Its register disposition is the single best term-contrast fact available anywhere in the corpus — 'Revoked by: EO 14003, January 22, 2021 / Reinstated by: EO 14171, January 20, 2025' — a first-term order struck out by the successor and restored on the first day of the current term, which is exactly what a term filter is for. It is not filed because db/issue-keys.json has no key for civil-service or executive-branch personnel control. The available near-misses are wrong in specific ways: cut_spending is a claim about money and this order changes an employment classification, and mapping it there would put a spending direction on a document whose text does not contain one; gov_waste carries no stated position for this figure, so the row would be coverage with nothing to test. Fail closed. The fix is an issue key, not a mapping. (8) The rescission of DACA — signed by the Acting Secretary of Homeland Security, not by the President. This file records what the figure did, and an agency memorandum is not his document. (9) Proclamation 9645, the entry restrictions. immigration_reform's stated position is about earned status for long-settled immigrants; entry restrictions are a different question, and mapping one onto the other to fill an empty issue would be the inference this lane refuses.
wave7.whatDidNotChange: border_security, end_dei, energy_production and climate_action still read as fully aligned after this wave and are reported that way. This wave was not a balance pass — wave 6 was — and the two contradictions it does produce (S.J. Res. 7 and S.J. Res. 68 against america_first_fp, and the CARES Act against cut_spending) are the consequence of what the documents say, not the purpose of selecting them. Four of the five stated positions those documents were checked against were written from 2024 platform material and 2025 second-term orders; none of the eight documents here is named or cited by any stance card, so no circularWithStance flag was needed anywhere in this wave. That was checked against the card text and source URL of every issue touched, not assumed.

wave8.purpose: RECENCY. Before this wave the newest action on file was Proclamation 11038, signed June 29, 2026, and the newest executive order was EO 14399, signed March 31, 2026 — so the order stream, which is the bulk of this lane, stopped four months before the profile was being read. A reader who knows the Federal Register would have seen a dead zone. _circularityRule.why: WHY SOME MAPPINGS CARRY circularWithStance. PDXWordAction's third rule is that a position is never its own test. word-action.js#isIndependentWord already catches the blatant form of the violation — a card that leads with a record verb AND cites the clerk or congress.gov. What it cannot catch is a card that asserts a view in the figure's own voice and then cites the very document that would test it, which is the NORMAL shape of a presidential stance card: these cards were largely written FROM this record. Left alone, feeding these actions into the consistency engine would have produced a dense, near-total agreement read that measured nothing except the fact that a card and its own source agree.
_circularityRule.howItIsApplied: The flag sits on an action→issue PAIR, not on an action and not on an issue. That is the whole point: a stance stays testable by a DIFFERENT document. energy_production is flagged against Executive Order 14154 and Executive Order 14156, whose titles its card quotes, and is scored against Public Law 119-21, which its card does not mention. consistency.js pairs this declared flag with a mechanical identifier match over the card's own text and evidence (order number, public-law number, measure number, exact title) and suppresses scoring when EITHER signal fires, so a later card rewrite that starts naming a document is caught without anyone remembering to edit this file.
_circularityRule.whatAFlagDoesNotDo: A flagged pair still ships and still counts as coverage — it is real, sourced record, and the lane renders it. It simply cannot be scored. The reader sees the action and the position side by side and is told the position was written from that action, which is more honest than either hiding the action or counting it as a match.
_circularityRule.whyNotJustDeleteThoseMappings: Because the mapping is true. Public Law 119-1 really does advance deportations; the flag records why that true mapping cannot serve as evidence about this particular figure's consistency, which is a different claim. Deleting it would lose real record to protect a score.

trump.title: Minimizing the Economic Burden of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act Pending Repeal

issues.plain: Told every agency with authority under the Affordable Care Act to waive, delay or grant exemptions from any of its requirements that impose a cost or a penalty, while repeal was pursued. That loosens the coverage law's reach without Congress changing it.
issues.rationale: Section 1 states the policy of seeking the prompt repeal of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, and section 2 directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services and every other agency with authority under the Act to 'waive, defer, grant exemptions from, or delay the implementation of' any provision imposing a cost, fee, tax, penalty or regulatory burden. Narrowing the reach of the coverage law is what this direction means on this issue.

trump._issuesNote: This is the first-term document behind the promise the roster records as broken — repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act. It is filed for that reason and it does not move the score: the stated position on healthcare is not directional, so the row lands in 'action on file, no stated position', exactly as the second-term healthcare actions do. What it changes is the standing column. Before this wave every healthcare document on file stood; now the issue holds one that was revoked outright, and that is visible in the term contrast rather than in the percentage. NOT mapped to healthcare_costs or health_drug_prices: the order directs relief from the Act's burdens on insurers, providers and device makers, and reading a household-price direction out of that would be the contested economic inference the lane refuses.

trump.title: Promoting Accountability and Streamlining Removal Procedures Consistent With Merit System Principles
trump._whyThisRow: THE OLDEST DOCUMENT UNDER THE NEW KEY, and the one that shows the key is not a synonym for Schedule F. This order creates no schedule and moves no position between services. What it does is narrow the removal and adverse-action procedures attached to executive-branch employees, which is the second limb of the key's scope note and the reason that limb is written the way it is. Filed with a rescinded standing: it did not survive the change of administration, and unlike Executive Order 13957 the register records no reinstatement of it.

issues.plain: Barred agencies from agreeing to progressive-discipline steps or grievance rights before removing a career employee, and held the period to fix performance to 30 days. It moves control over firings from negotiated procedure to the agency head.
issues.rationale: Section 2 sets the principles: agencies should limit the opportunity period to demonstrate acceptable performance under 5 U.S.C. 4302(c)(6) to the time that provides sufficient opportunity, supervisors and deciding officials should not be required to use progressive discipline, and agencies should not require suspension of an employee before proposing to remove that employee. Section 4 then makes those principles binding: no agency shall make an agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, that limits its discretion to employ chapter 75 procedures to address unacceptable performance, that requires chapter 43 procedures before removing an employee for unacceptable performance, or that limits its discretion to remove an employee from Federal service without first engaging in progressive discipline, and section 4(c) holds the demonstration period to 30 days except where the agency determines in its sole and exclusive discretion that longer is necessary. Section 3 directs agency heads to endeavor to exclude from grievance procedures negotiated under 5 U.S.C. 7121 any dispute concerning decisions to remove an employee from Federal service. The instrument narrows the adverse-action protections attached to career executive-branch employees, which is what this key records.

trump._issuesNote: ONE ISSUE, DELIBERATELY. Section 3 and section 4(a) touch federal-sector bargaining, which is the ground on which Executive Orders 13836 and 13837 of the same day were rejected from this wave. They are not mapped here either: the direction that matters in this document is what it does to removal procedure, and bargaining is the vehicle rather than the subject. There is no second issue on this row because there is no honest second one — this is a personnel-procedure instrument and reading a spending or workforce-size direction out of it would be the inference the lane refuses.

trump.title: Creating Schedule F in the Excepted Service
trump._whyThisRow: THE DOCUMENT THIS WHOLE PASS EXISTS FOR. Wave 7 reviewed it, wanted it, and refused it in writing: 'It is not filed because db/issue-keys.json has no key for civil-service or executive-branch personnel control ... Fail closed. The fix is an issue key, not a mapping.' The key now exists, so the document lands. Its register record is the sharpest term-contrast fact anywhere in the corpus — revoked by the succeeding President and reinstated on the first day of the next term — and it is filed with three status rows because no single row can carry that.

issues.plain: Created Schedule F, moving career federal jobs that shape policy into the excepted service and switching off the civil-service hiring and removal rules for them. Making those posts removable at will is what this issue is about.
issues.rationale: Section 3 directs that appointments to positions of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating character that are not normally subject to change as a result of a Presidential transition shall be made under Schedule F of the excepted service. Section 4(a)(i) amends 5 CFR 6.2 to add that schedule to the list of positions OPM excepts from the competitive service, defining it as 'Positions of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character not normally subject to change as a result of a Presidential transition'. Section 4(a)(ii) amends 5 CFR 6.4 to read that, except as required by statute, 'the Civil Service Rules and Regulations shall not apply to removals from positions listed in Schedules A, C, D, E, or F'. Section 1 states the finding it rests on: that conditions of good administration make necessary an exception to the competitive hiring rules and examinations for career positions of that character, and similarly make necessary excepting such positions from the adverse action procedures set forth in chapter 75 of title 5. Creating an excepted category for career policy-influencing positions and detaching the removal rules from it is the mechanism this key exists to record.

trump._issuesNote: The order is about the classification of career positions and nothing else, so it carries one issue. It is NOT mapped to cut_spending, which wave 7 named as the near-miss and rejected: cut_spending is a claim about money and this text contains no spending direction. It is NOT mapped to gov_waste or to any broad government-reform key, because a key that can absorb a reclassification order can absorb anything and would stop meaning anything. trump.title: William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021
trump._whyThisRow: WAVE 9, AND THE ROW THE overridden TOKEN EXISTS FOR. Wave 7 put three vetoes on file and every one of them held — each carries a single in_force standing recording an override attempt that fell short. That is a true record of those three documents and a false picture of the veto power on this profile, because the one veto of this presidency that Congress DID override was left out. It was left out for a reason wave 7 stated: the vocabulary had no way to say it. in_force asserts the veto held; blocked and struck_down name a court; superseded names a later presidential action. The token was added in this pass so the row could be filed honestly, and this is the only row that uses it — see _verificationPass.wave9 for the proof that no second example exists in either term.
trump._citationNote: congress.gov is the source of record for this class per db/exec-action-types.json#actionClasses.vetoed_law and returns HTTP 403 to this environment, so every fact asserted here was read from documents that do answer, and each is named where it is used: the veto message from GovInfo's Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents (DCPD-202000903), the House override from the Clerk of the House's own roll-call record for the 116th Congress (roll 253 of 2020), the Senate override from the Senate's roll-call record (vote 292 of the 2nd session of the 116th Congress), and the enactment from GPO's published enrolled text of Public Law 116-283. The enrolled text is the strongest of the four: it prints both reconsideration resolutions verbatim and its LEGISLATIVE HISTORY block names the December 23 veto message, the December 28 House override and the January 1 Senate override.

issues.plain: Vetoed the annual defense authorization, returning the Pentagon's funding levels and troop strengths to the House unsigned rather than enacting them.
issues.counts: The stated position pairs America First with backing the armed forces, and the annual defense authorization is the bill that sets the Pentagon's funding levels and troop strengths. That is why an action taken on it is filed here.
issues.rationale: The direction recorded here describes the MEASURE, not the action taken against it. H.R. 6395 is the annual defense authorization: its long title is 'An Act to authorize appropriations for fiscal year 2021 for military activities of the Department of Defense, for military construction, and for defense activities of the Department of Energy, to prescribe military personnel strengths for such fiscal year, and for other purposes'. Funding and manning the armed forces at the level the Department asked for is what the stated position's commitment to the military is about, so the measure advances this issue. The record engine inverts a blocking action, so the veto itself reads the other way — it returned that authorization to the House without approval.

trump._issuesNote: ONE MAPPING, AND THE TENSION IN IT IS DISCLOSED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER. This lane reports what an action did to a measure, not the reasons given for it, and the two point different ways here more sharply than on any other row in the file. The veto message's own words are 'My Administration recognizes the importance of the Act to our national security' and 'No one has worked harder, or approved more money for the military, than I have'; the objections it raises are to the absence of a repeal of Section 230, to a provision renaming military installations, to limits on military construction funds, to a 5G provision, and to restrictions on withdrawing troops from Afghanistan, Germany and South Korea. None of those is a rejection of the authorization levels. The row still reads as an action against the issue because that is what the veto did to the measure, and a reader who wants the reasons has the veto message linked on the row. WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT MAPPED: america_first_fp. The argument for it is real — the Act's restrictions on troop drawdowns cut against an 'end the open-ended commitments' position, so the veto would read as advancing it — but this pass did not read those sections of a 4,517-page Act, and the veto message's characterisation of them is not a reading of them. Fail closed: a second mapping asserted from a summary would be exactly the soft approximation this pass was told to avoid, and it would have had the convenient effect of making the row read both ways.

Section 4 directs the Director of the Office of Personnel Management to amend the Civil Service Regulations to rescind the changes made by the final rule of April 9, 2024, 89 Fed. Reg. 24982, that impede the purposes of Executive Order 13957, and holds 5 CFR part 302 subpart F and 5 CFR 210.102(b)(3) and (4) inoperative until that is done. Section 6 revokes Executive Order 14003, the order that had revoked Executive Order 13957. It carries the heaviest weight under this key because it is the instrument that put the category back.

issues.plain: Imposed an extra across-the-board duty on goods from China, using emergency economic powers after finding ordinary tariff authority inadequate.
issues.counts: This issue asks whether tariffs are actually used against China. The order puts an additional duty on every article that is a product of the PRC, reaching for emergency economic powers after finding ordinary tariff authority inadequate.
issues.rationale: Imposes an additional ad valorem duty on all articles that are products of the People's Republic of China, invoking section 1702(a)(1)(B) of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act on the finding that other tariff authority was inadequate.

issues.plain: Set the China duty rate himself by executive order under emergency economic powers, rather than under a rate schedule enacted by Congress.

trump.title: Adjusting Imports of Steel Into the United States
trump._whyThisOneMattersMost: Five of this profile's tariff issues rested on ONE document, Executive Order 14257 — and on February 20, 2026 the Supreme Court held that the statute that order was issued under does not authorise tariffs at all. A whole quadrant of the record was one ruling away from having nothing testable in it. This proclamation is issued under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, a delegation Congress wrote, and it is untouched by that ruling and by Executive Order 14389, which ended the duties imposed under the emergency statute. The tariff record now has a second leg that does not depend on the first.

issues.plain: Terminated every country arrangement, exemption and quota that had displaced the steel tariff — Canada, Mexico, the EU, Japan, the UK, Brazil and others — restoring the duty across steel imports.
issues.counts: Steel is the domestic industry this tariff was built to protect. Ending every country arrangement, exemption and quota puts the duty back across the whole steel import base, which is the protection this issue measures.
issues.rationale: Terminates every country arrangement, exemption and quota that had displaced the section 232 steel tariff — for South Korea, Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Mexico, the European Union, Japan, the United Kingdom and Ukraine — effective March 12, 2025, restoring the ad valorem duty across steel imports.

issues.plain: Uses a duty on one industrial input to rebuild domestic steel capacity, and closes the side doors named partners had been shipping through.
issues.rationale: Uses import duties on a single industrial input as the instrument for rebuilding domestic steel capacity, and removes the alternative arrangements that had let named partners ship outside the duty.

issues.plain: Restores the duty across the steel import base with no offsetting relief for the American manufacturers and builders who buy steel.
issues.counts: Steel is an input, not a shelf good: the duty is paid by the American manufacturers and builders who buy it. This proclamation restores it across the import base with nothing offsetting it for them, and that downstream cost is what this issue tracks.
issues.rationale: Restores the duty across the steel import base with no offsetting relief for downstream purchasers.

trump._issuesNote: NOT mapped to tariffs_authority, and the omission is the point of the row. That issue is about setting tariffs without Congress; this proclamation acts under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which is a delegation Congress enacted. Carrying it there would file a use of congressional authority as evidence of bypassing Congress.

issues.plain: Directed the federal government into the running of elections that the Constitution leaves to the states — setting a ballot-receipt rule and conditioning federal election funding on state compliance.
issues.counts: Running elections is the textbook case of a power left to the states. This order directs it from Washington — a ballot-receipt rule enforced against states, and federal election money conditioned on adopting a registration form the order rewrote.

Mapped opposes on the chip "keep decisions with the states unless there’s a clear national reason for Washington to override them," which the order overrides by directing state election administration from Washington. Note the standing rows already on this document: a federal court has permanently enjoined parts of it. This mapping records what the order directed, and the standing rows record what survived.

trump.title: Regulating Imports With a Reciprocal Tariff To Rectify Trade Practices That Contribute to Large and Persistent Annual United States Goods Trade Deficits
trump._whyThisOneMattersMost: The largest single gap the audit found. Five of this president's stated positions are about tariffs — two of them written in the protective direction, so a tariff order tests them by opposing them — and before this row the lane had no tariff document at all and reported 'no action on file yet' on every one of them. One of those cards names this order by its number, which is exactly why the circularity guard has to run per pair rather than per document: the card that names it cannot be tested by it, and the four that do not name it can.

issues.plain: Imposed a baseline duty on imports from nearly every trading partner plus higher country-specific rates, on the finding that persistent goods deficits hollowed out domestic manufacturing.
issues.counts: This issue asks whether tariffs are put to work rebuilding domestic manufacturing, and that is the order's own stated ground: persistent goods trade deficits had hollowed out the manufacturing base.
issues.rationale: Imposes a baseline ad valorem duty on imports from nearly all trading partners plus higher country-specific rates, on the stated ground that persistent goods trade deficits have hollowed out the domestic manufacturing base.
issues._circularNote: The circular hold on this mapping was lifted. It was held because the tariffs_growth stance card named this order by number and by date — "he signed Executive Order 14257 on April 2, 2025" — which both the declared flag and the mechanical guard in consistency.js#execCircular caught. That card has been re-authored from the 2024 Republican Party Platform he campaigned on, whose trade chapter states the baseline-tariff position without reference to any order, so neither signal fires and this document can test it.

issues.plain: Sets the rates by executive order under emergency economic powers rather than under a rate schedule enacted by Congress.
issues.rationale: Sets tariff rates by executive order under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act rather than under a rate schedule enacted by Congress.
issues._circularNote: The circular hold on this mapping was lifted. It was held because the tariffs_authority stance card was written about the litigation over this very order — it described the first presidential invocation of IEEPA to set tariffs and cited the Supreme Court opinion in the case challenging it — and, no identifier matching mechanically, the declared flag was the only thing holding the pair. That card has been re-authored from his own September 2024 campaign remarks that he does not need Congress to impose tariffs, a statement that predates this order and does not depend on it, so this document can test it.

issues.plain: The duties reach nearly the whole import base and the order pairs them with no offsetting relief for household purchasers.
issues.counts: This issue asks who pays for a tariff. The duties reach nearly the entire import base and the order carries no offsetting measure for household purchasers, so the charge lands on the buyer.
issues.rationale: The duties apply across nearly the whole import base and the order pairs them with no offsetting relief for household purchasers.

issues.plain: Assigns China one of the higher country-specific rates in the annexed schedule, on the stated ground of non-reciprocal trade practices.
issues.counts: The reciprocal tariff is a global instrument, and its China reading is one of the six issues it is judged on: the annexed schedule assigns the PRC one of the higher country-specific rates rather than the baseline.
issues.rationale: Assigns China one of the higher country-specific rates in the annexed schedule, on the stated ground of non-reciprocal trade practices.

issues.plain: Uses import duties as the instrument for reshoring manufacturing and rebuilding supply chains.
issues.rationale: Uses import duties as the instrument for reshoring domestic manufacturing and rebuilding supply chains.

issues.plain: The duty reaches articles from nearly every trading partner and the order pairs it with no offsetting relief, so the charge lands on imported consumer goods — one of the four costs the day-one affordability directive named.
issues.counts: The affordability directive on file named consumer goods as one of four costs to bring down. This order puts a duty on articles from nearly every trading partner with nothing offsetting it for households, which reaches that category directly.
issues.rationale: The stated position on this chip is the day-one directive telling every agency to pursue emergency measures lowering the cost of housing, health care, energy and consumer goods. This order runs the other way on the last of those: it imposes an additional ad valorem duty on articles from nearly every trading partner, with higher country-specific rates in its annex, and it contains no offsetting measure for household purchasers. Added in wave 12 as a secondary mapping at reduced weight because the order is a trade instrument whose stated subject is the goods trade deficit rather than consumer prices; the tariffs_prices mapping already on this row carries the narrow reading about tariffs and prices, and this one carries the separate tension with the affordability directive. Note the struck_down standing row already on this document: this mapping records what the order imposed, and the standing rows record what survived.

trump.title: Assuring the Security of the State of Qatar
trump._whyThisRow: WAVE 12 — THE COUNTER-DIRECTIONAL GAP ON THE WAR LANE. Before this wave the restraint row carried exactly two documents and the war_powers row the same two, both of them term-45 vetoes, and neither issue carried a single instrument from the second term. This order was read from its own published text in this pass and it is the plainest second-term instrument on those issues: it commits the United States in advance to defend another state, including by military means, and it does so by order alone, naming no treaty, statute or authorization for the use of military force anywhere in its text. It is filed because leaving it out is what let the foreign-policy lane read in one direction, not because of where its direction lands.

issues.plain: Committed the United States in advance to defend another country by military means if that country is attacked, and set up standing joint war planning to carry it out — a forward commitment made by order alone, with no congressional authorization named in it.
issues.rationale: Section 1 makes it the policy of the United States “to guarantee the security and territorial integrity of the State of Qatar against external attack.” Section 2(a) provides that the United States “shall regard any armed attack on the territory, sovereignty, or critical infrastructure of the State of Qatar as a threat to the peace and security of the United States,” and section 2(b) that in that event the United States “shall take all lawful and appropriate measures—including diplomatic, economic, and, if necessary, military—to defend the interests of the United States and of the State of Qatar and to restore peace and stability.” Section 2(c) directs the Secretary of War, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Director of National Intelligence, to “maintain joint contingency planning” with Qatar for a rapid and coordinated response. The order rests on “the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States” and identifies no treaty, statute or authorization for the use of military force. Mapped as opposing the congressional war-power chip because the instrument is itself the whole authorization for what it promises.

issues.plain: A standing promise to fight for another country if it is attacked is a new open-ended military commitment, not the winding down of one.
issues.counts: This issue tracks whether commitments abroad are being wound down or added to. The order adds one: guaranteeing another state's security becomes United States policy, on a trigger no narrower than any armed attack, with no end date behind it.
issues.rationale: Sections 1 and 2, quoted in the war_powers rationale on this row. Filed against the restraint chip because the commitment the order creates carries no end date, no sunset and no triggering condition narrower than “any armed attack” on the covered state’s territory, sovereignty or critical infrastructure, and because section 2(c) makes the planning for it continuous rather than contingent on a later decision. The mapping records what the order commits the United States to do; it makes no claim about whether that commitment was wise.

issues.plain: The stated doctrine presses allies to carry more of their own defense; this order has the United States take on the defense of one instead. A narrower link — the order is a security guarantee, not a foreign-aid or burden-sharing instrument.
issues.counts: The doctrine on file presses allies to carry more of their own defense. This order runs the other way for one of them — the United States guarantees that state's security, and the order asks nothing in return and sets no cost-sharing condition.
issues.rationale: The stated position on this chip is a doctrine of pressing allies to fund their own defense and of questioning open-ended commitments abroad. Section 1 of this order runs the other way for one ally: it makes guaranteeing that state’s security and territorial integrity the policy of the United States, and section 2(b) puts American military means behind the guarantee if an attack comes. The order asks nothing of the covered state in return and sets no cost-sharing condition. Mapped below the weight given to the war_powers reading because the stated doctrine is written about aid and burden-sharing rather than about defense guarantees, so the tension is real but secondary.

trump._whyThisRow: WAVE 6 — COUNTER-DIRECTIONAL. Every tariff issue on this profile pointed one way. econ_trade, tariffs_china and tariffs_growth held only documents that impose tariffs; tariffs_prices held only documents that push against its protective chip. A record in which a president never once narrowed his own signature tariff is not a record of tariff policy, it is a record of the documents that were collected. This is the president narrowing it, on his own initiative, four months before the Supreme Court reached the statute: he took agricultural products out of the Executive Order 14257 reciprocal tariff outright, backdated the exclusion by a day, and ordered refunds of duties already collected. Nothing compelled it.

issues.plain: Pulled a list of agricultural products out of the reciprocal tariff and ordered refunds of duties already collected on them.
issues.counts: Pulling farm goods out of the reciprocal tariff, and refunding duties already collected on them, takes the tariff component back out of what those imports cost — the direct form of relief this issue measures.
issues.rationale: Section 1 determines that certain agricultural products shall not be subject to the reciprocal tariff imposed under Executive Order 14257, as amended, and issues updated versions of that order's Annex II; section 2 modifies the Harmonized Tariff Schedule accordingly effective for goods entered on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on November 13, 2025 — a day before signature — and provides that to the extent implementation requires a refund of duties collected, refunds shall be processed through U.S. Customs and Border Protection's standard procedures.

issues.plain: Narrows the reciprocal tariff's coverage, giving domestic demand and domestic production capacity — not a concession from a trading partner — as part of the reason.
issues.counts: The carve-out is filed on the industry question, and not only on the price rows, because the order gives domestic production capacity as part of its reason — goods the country does not make enough of come out of the tariff, rather than the tariff being used to build that capacity.
issues.rationale: Removes a class of goods from the reciprocal tariff's coverage, and gives as the grounds for doing so the President's consideration of "current domestic demand for certain products, and current domestic capacity to produce certain products" alongside the status of negotiations — a narrowing of the instrument driven in part by domestic supply conditions rather than by anything a trading partner conceded.

issues.plain: Took the reciprocal-tariff duty back off imported food — coffee, bananas, beef and other farm goods the United States does not grow enough of — so the tariff stopped showing up in grocery prices.
issues.counts: Groceries are the consumer-goods category the affordability directive named, and this is the only instrument in the record that reaches food prices directly — coffee, bananas and beef come back out of the tariff, with refunds for duties already collected.
issues.rationale: Section 2 modifies the Harmonized Tariff Schedule as provided in Annex I, effective for goods entered for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on November 13, 2025, and provides for refunds of duties already collected. Section 1 states the decision followed monitoring of "current domestic demand for certain products, and current domestic capacity to produce certain products." Filed as a secondary mapping on a document already in this record for its tariffs_prices and tariffs_growth mappings: the household-grocery reading is a distinct issue from the general price reading, and this is the only instrument in the record that reaches food prices directly.

trump._issuesNote: NOT mapped to econ_trade. That chip is about using tariffs and trade rules to defend American manufacturing, and the order's own stated reason for the carve-out is domestic capacity to produce the goods — it reaches products the United States does not make in quantity, so reading it as a retreat from defending American manufacturing would be reading the direction of the instrument rather than the document. NOT mapped to tariffs_authority: the order acts under the same emergency statute as the tariff it narrows, so it is not evidence about Congress's role either way. NOT mapped to cost_living: that issue already holds three same-direction documents and a fourth would add weight without adding a test, which is what this wave exists to avoid.

trump.title: Safeguarding Venezuelan Oil Revenue for the Good of the American and Venezuelan People
trump._whyThisRow: WAVE 12. The america_first_fp row read at full confidence on two same-day January 2025 orders that cut the same way, and on nothing since. This order is the second-term instrument that cuts the other way, and its own findings are what make it so: it declares a new national emergency in order to hold another government’s oil revenue in United States custody, and it names ensuring that country’s economic and political stability, and bringing peace and prosperity to its people and to the hemisphere, among the major foreign policy objectives of the United States. Filed for its text, not for its direction.
trump._issuesNote: NOT mapped to energy_production: the order governs the custody of sale proceeds already held by the Treasury and directs no domestic production. NOT mapped to immig_fentanyl or tough_on_crime: the section 1 findings mention narcotics flows among the objectives the order says it protects, but the operative sections reach only attachment, transfer and custody of funds, and a mapping has to rest on what an instrument does.

issues.plain: Declared a new national emergency so the United States could hold another government's oil revenue in Treasury custody, and named that country's economic and political stability an American foreign policy objective the order says must not fail.
issues.counts: This issue tracks open-ended commitments abroad. The order makes another country's economic and political stability a named United States objective and puts the Treasury in custody of that country's oil revenue, for a period the order does not bound.
issues.rationale: Section 1 finds that attachment or other judicial process against the covered funds “will substantially interfere with our critical efforts to ensure economic and political stability in Venezuela,” and that the failure of those efforts “would jeopardize major foreign policy objectives of the United States,” which the section lists as ending illegal immigration and illicit narcotics flows, “protecting American interests against malign actors such as Iran and Hezbollah,” and “bringing peace, prosperity, and stability to the Venezuelan people and to the Western Hemisphere more generally.” On that finding the order declares a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act. Section 3 renders any attachment, judgment, lien, execution or garnishment against the covered funds null and void and bars any transfer of them except under a licence issued under the order. Section 4 finds the funds are property of that government, held by the United States “solely in a custodial and governmental capacity,” and “held pending sovereign disposition for public, governmental, or diplomatic purposes determined by the Secretary of State, on behalf of the Government of Venezuela.” Mapped as opposing the America-First chip because that chip is written around questioning open-ended commitments abroad, and this order takes one on: it makes another country’s stabilization a named United States objective and puts the Treasury in the position of custodian for that country’s resource revenue for a period the order does not bound.

trump.title: Ensuring Affordable Beef for the American Consumer
trump._whyThisRow: cost_living was the other fully-held issue. Its only document was the day-one memorandum, and the stance card on the issue quotes that memorandum by title, so the pair is circular and the issue read as no record. The memorandum names four cost categories — housing, health care, food and energy. This is a formal action inside one of them, signed thirteen months later, that no card names.

issues.plain: Raised the 2026 beef import quota by 80,000 metric tons of lean trimmings, released quarterly and allocated to Argentina, on a determination that domestic supply would not meet demand at reasonable prices.
issues.counts: A formal supply action aimed at making a staple consumer food more affordable.
issues.rationale: Increases the calendar-year 2026 in-quota quantity of the beef tariff-rate quota by 80,000 metric tons of lean beef trimmings, released in four quarterly tranches and allocated in its entirety to Argentina, on the determination that domestic supply would otherwise be inadequate to meet domestic demand at reasonable prices.

issues.plain: Enlarging the quota lets that beef enter at the low in-quota tariff rate instead of the high over-quota rate — a trade barrier lowered to hold a grocery price down.
issues.counts: A tariff barrier lowered for the stated purpose of holding a consumer price down — the exact trade-off this issue is about.
issues.rationale: Lowers a tariff barrier for the stated purpose of holding a consumer price down: the proclamation enlarges the in-quota quantity so that beef entering under the quota pays the low in-quota rate rather than the over-quota rate, on the President's determination that domestic supply would otherwise be inadequate to meet domestic demand at reasonable prices.

trump._issuesNote: WAVE 6 ADDS THE tariffs_prices MAPPING THAT WAVE 5 DECLINED TO WRITE. Wave 5's note read: 'NOT mapped to econ_trade or any tariffs_* issue, although the instrument is a tariff-rate quota. The proclamation lowers a trade barrier to bring a consumer price down, which is the opposite direction from every tariff document on this profile; filing it under a tariff issue would make the trade record read as though it pointed both ways on the strength of one grocery measure.' That refusal was correct on wave 5's evidence and its stated condition is now met, not waived. Wave 6 adds two further barrier-lowering documents — Executive Order 14360, which took agricultural products out of the reciprocal tariff outright with refunds, and Proclamation 11038, which suspends collection of countervailing duties on Moroccan phosphate fertilizer — so the direction is no longer carried by one grocery measure. The tariffs_prices chip states the PROTECTIVE position (pair tariffs with exemptions or relief so everyday costs do not rise), and lowering a barrier to hold a price down is what that chip describes. STILL not mapped to econ_trade or tariffs_growth: those chips are about defending American manufacturing and reshoring it, and cattle ranching is not what either names.

trump.title: Ending Certain Tariff Actions
trump._whyNoTariffsAuthorityMapping: This order was read in full for a tariffs_authority mapping and deliberately does not carry one. Ending the duties does not return anything to Congress: the order is issued under the same International Emergency Economic Powers Act authority as the orders it unwinds, it states that the underlying national emergencies "remain in effect and shall not be affected by this order," and nothing in it disclaims the power to reimpose the duties tomorrow by the same instrument. The chip for that issue is about WHO DECIDES, and on that question this document moves nothing. Mapping it "advances" would have preserved a clean full-confidence read on that row by reading a rate change as a separation-of-powers change, which is the verdict-friendly selection this pass exists to avoid. The instrument is in the record; the direction is left off, and this note is the reason.

issues.plain: Ended the tariffs he had imposed on China under emergency economic powers, ordering agencies to stop collecting them as soon as practicable.
issues.counts: The duties this order ends include the ones on PRC goods imposed under Executive Order 14195 — the instrument that built this issue's record — so stopping their collection lands directly on it.
issues.rationale: Section 1 provides that the additional ad valorem duties imposed under IEEPA in Executive Order 14195 as amended — the synthetic-opioid duties on the PRC — along with those in Executive Orders 14193, 14194, 14245, 14257, 14323, 14329, 14380 and 14382, "shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as practicable, shall no longer be collected." Section 2(a) directs every agency head to "take all appropriate steps to end" those duties and to "immediately begin taking steps to effectuate this order."

issues.plain: Switched off the whole emergency-powers tariff program at once, removing the import duties that were the instrument of the reshoring case.
issues.counts: Tariffs are the instrument the reshoring case on this issue rests on. This order switches nine of them off at once, the reciprocal tariff among them.
issues.rationale: Section 1, above, reaches nine orders including Executive Order 14257, the reciprocal-tariff order whose stated ground was that persistent goods trade deficits had hollowed out the domestic manufacturing base. Mapped opposes because the chip is about USING tariffs to reshore manufacturing and this instrument ends their collection.

issues.plain: Removing the duties takes the tariff component back out of the price of the covered imports.
issues.counts: This issue is about what a tariff adds at the till. Ending collection across nine orders, with refunds processed for duties already paid, removes that addition from every import those orders covered.
issues.rationale: Section 1 ends collection of the additional ad valorem duties; section 2(b) directs the Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of Homeland Security and the United States Trade Representative to implement, and section 2(a) provides for refunds of duties collected to be processed under standard Customs procedures. Mapped advances because the chip asks that families be shielded from tariff-driven price increases.
